newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians march for peace through capital.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians march for peace through capital.

text.p: Some 1,300 people, led by hundreds of Buddhist monks and nuns, marched through central Phnom Penh on Sunday to urge Cambodia's political leaders to resolve problems without resorting to violence.

The peace march was organised by a prominent Buddhist monk, the Venerable Maha Ghosananda, and came four weeks after the city was rocked by two days of battles when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted his senior coalition partner, Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
"We want to see the Cambodian leaders who are arguing calm down and avoid violence," 26-year-old Buddhist monk Peah Savorn told Reuters.

The procession passed without incident. Co-Interior Minister Sar Kheng, a senior member of Hun Sen's party, joined the march at its conclusion and told reporters it was a significant event and he agreed with the call for peace.

Many foreign aid workers joined the march, and U.S. Ambassador Kenneth Quinn spoke to some participants at the city's Independence Monument where the procession ended and the marchers meditated for three minutes.
Organiser Thida Khus said the message of peace was directed at Cambodia's political leaders as well as ordinary people.
"The main purpose of this march is to convey the message, not only to the people but the government, we want to see Cambodian leaders resolving their problems peacefully," she said.
Some 60 people were killed and up to 200 wounded when forces loyal to the rival premiers battled in the capital a month ago. Most of the casualties were civilians caught in the crossfire.
Human rights workers say about 40 opposition figures were killed in a subsequent crackdown against the ousted prince's party.
Forces loyal to the two prime ministers have clashed intermittently in parts of northern and northwestern Cambodia since Ranariddh's ouster.
